chunks: Bandwidth versus sampling rate. The question: What is the difference between bandwidth and sampling rate?
These are two separate limits on a measuring instrument. Bandwidth is analog: it says how fast a wiggle the input circuitry can pass along before the signal starts shrinking.
Sample rate is digital: it says how many times per second the converter records the voltage. They must be matched.
If frequencies get through that are too fast for the sample rate, they show up as false, slower signals.
Film a spinning wheel with a camera that takes 24 pictures a second.
If the wheel turns about once per picture, each frame looks almost the same as the last, so the wheel seems slow or even backward.
That is aliasing, and the frame rate is the sample rate. Bandwidth is like a guard in front of the camera who stops very fast spinning from reaching it at all.
bandwidth lives in the analog block (B), sample rate in the converter (C). Anything that gets past B is seen by C; whatever C cannot represent folds down.
Bandwidth: the frequency where the instrument's response has dropped to about 70% of the amplitude (-3 decibels). Sample rate: how many samples per second the converter takes.
Nyquist frequency: half the sample rate, the highest frequency that can be recorded without ambiguity.
Aliasing: a fast signal appearing as a false, lower frequency because of too little sampling.
Anti-alias filter: an analog filter placed before the converter to remove frequencies above the Nyquist frequency.
Sample a 900 hertz tone at 1000 samples per second. The Nyquist frequency is 500 hertz, so 900 hertz is too high.
The samples look exactly like those of a 100 hertz tone, because 900 minus 1000 equals 100 . Nothing in the data tells you the tone was really 900 hertz.
The fix is to remove the 900 hertz before sampling with a filter, or to sample faster than 1800 samples per second. That is the whole idea.
"Bandwidth is the analog front end's limit: the frequency where amplitude has dropped 3 decibels.
Sample rate is how often the ADC samples, and Nyquist says you can only represent frequencies below half of it.
They're separate but linked: anything above half the sample rate that gets through the front end aliases down to a false lower frequency, so the bandwidth or anti-alias filter must cut it first.
Scopes typically sample at 2. 5 to 5 times their bandwidth, giving margin and enough points to reconstruct the waveform."
